Isoform switching after LPS, and what UBL5 loss does to it

Analysis summary — state of the project

Author

Project

Published

August 22, 2026

WarningScope of this document

This report covers scripts 00–07. It predates the layer-decoupling, hidden-layer and GFF3 event-structure work (scripts 08–10 and docs/external_review/), and does not include those results.

Claims corrected since the first version, now reflected in the text below: the Q2 response-magnitude stratification conditions on a mediator and does not explain the deficit away; the 35% same-sample figure is a reference point, not a reproducibility ceiling; the H-vs-T switching contrast is retired (H_HT alone is batch-corrected).

Retracted elsewhere and never quoted here — the 64%/38% expression-vs-splicing layer asymmetry and its mediation split (an estimator artefact, scripts/10_layer_estimator_calibration.R), and the ISG “sparing” reading (a ratio-scale artefact). Full ledger: docs/AGENT_CONTEXT.md §“Retracted — do not cite” and docs/external_review/HANDOFF.md.

1 The question

Macrophages responding to LPS reprogram their transcriptome through TLR4 signalling. Most analyses of that response ask which genes change in abundance. This project asks a different question: which genes change which isoform they use, independent of whether total gene output goes up or down.

Two questions, on two reference transcriptomes:

  • Q1 — Does LPS drive isoform switching in wildtype THP-1? Anchored on T_HT, with H_HT as a supplementary genotype, both on the HT reference.
  • Q2 — Does losing UBL5 change post-LPS isoform selection? T_UT (wildtype) versus U_UT (UBL5 knockout), both on the UT reference.

UBL5 is the human homolog of yeast Hub1, a small ubiquitin-like protein associated with spliceosome function. That makes it a plausible modifier of isoform choice rather than of transcription per se — which is exactly what this design can test. (Framing taken from config/config.yml; the mechanistic rationale is worth confirming against the primary literature before it goes in a manuscript.)

NoteWhat this pipeline is and is not

This repository starts after IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR (ISA). It does not quantify reads or run the differential test — it consumes saved switchAnalyzeRlist objects and does the downstream comparison, ranking, and visualisation. Every significance call here was made upstream; what changed during this work is how those calls are filtered, counted, compared, and displayed.

2 Design and data

Both references are PacBio-augmented: long-read transcripts were merged with the reference annotation, so a large fraction of transcript models are novel (PB-prefixed). Three replicates per condition.

2.1 A structural feature of the inputs that shapes everything downstream

The four primary ISA objects were each saved after reduceToSwitchingGenes = TRUE, so every gene inside them already passes the gene-level significance cutoff. This is not an error — it is the ISA default — but it means “genes in the object” is a set already selected on the outcome.

All four datasets now have an unfiltered export, so the real denominator is recoverable throughout: 8.2k–12.0k genes tested per dataset, of which 16–25% switch. Those exports are used for display and classification only — every significance call still comes from the primary objects — but they are what makes any statement about a rate meaningful. Everything below states which denominator it uses.

3 Defining a switch

An isoform counts as switching when its q-value and its gene’s q-value are below 0.05 and |dIF| ≥ 0.15 — a shift of at least 15 percentage points in that isoform’s share of its gene’s expression.

The |dIF| floor is a judgement call, so it was scanned rather than assumed:

Note the honest caveat: because the inputs are pre-selected, this curve shows how the floor prunes an already-significant set. It is not a sensitivity/specificity curve, and should not be presented as one.

4 Q1 — LPS drives isoform switching in wildtype cells

In the wildtype anchor T_HT, 95 of 10,907 tested genes (0.9%) show at least one qualifying isoform switch.

These counts are lower than earlier versions of this report for two deliberate reasons, both documented in docs/REVIEW_CHANGES.md §0c: significance now comes from the unfiltered objects rather than being mixed across two FDR universes, and an abundance floor (gene expression ≥ 12) removes calls where isoform fraction is within replicate noise. About half the raw calls came from genes too lowly expressed to estimate a fraction reliably.

4.1 The top switching genes are bona fide LPS-response genes

This is the most reassuring result in the project. The ranking was produced by effect size and q-value with no knowledge of immunology, and it returns NCOA7, RSAD2, KDM6B, CMPK2, IFIT5, IRAK3, CCL3/CCL4, SIGLEC9 — interferon-stimulated genes, chemokines, a TLR-pathway negative regulator, and an LPS-induced chromatin modifier. Isoform switching is landing on the canonical LPS program, not on a random slice of the transcriptome.

5 Novel PacBio isoforms carry a large share of the switching

Because both references are long-read augmented, a natural question is whether novel transcripts are real participants or annotation noise.

Two observations:

  1. Novel isoforms are represented among switching events at least in proportion to their abundance, and in H_HT and U_UT somewhat above it (58.3% of switches from 36.2% of isoforms).
  2. Their effect sizes are indistinguishable from known isoforms — median |dIF| around 0.20–0.23 in both groups, in every dataset.

The class-code breakdown is worth pausing on: a substantial block are j — genuinely novel junction combinations — and these are the ones that would be invisible to a short-read-only annotation. That is the argument for the long-read reference paying off.

6 Q2 — UBL5 loss dampens LPS-driven isoform switching

This is where the unfiltered exports change what can be concluded.

6.1 Fewer genes switch in the knockout

Against the full tested background (not the pre-selected objects):

24.9% of tested genes switch in wildtype versus 16.4% in the knockout. Under the pre-selected objects this comparison was impossible — the denominators were 248 and 127 genes, both 100% significant by construction.

6.1.1 But the knockout’s whole LPS response runs at about half amplitude

Direction is preserved (Spearman 0.73) but amplitude is roughly halved (regression slope 0.516; the top 200 wildtype responders retain 58% of their response). This is a global transcriptional phenotype, not a splicing one.

It matters because a switch needs a condition-driven shift in isoform fraction to clear a fixed |dIF| ≥ 0.15. If the whole perturbation runs at half amplitude, fewer shifts clear the bar regardless of any splicing-specific role. Stratifying each gene by its own response magnitude:

ImportantThis stratification cannot settle Q2 — it conditions on a mediator

Crude odds ratio for switching, KO vs WT: 0.508. Adjusted for response magnitude (Mantel–Haenszel): 0.773, 95% CI 0.565–1.058, p = 0.114.

An earlier version of this document read that as the deficit being explained away. That reading is withdrawn. UBL5/Hub1 is a spliceosome-associated modifier. If splicing regulation is upstream of the LPS response, then response magnitude is a mediator, not a confounder — and conditioning on a mediator removes the very effect being measured. The arithmetic is correct; the causal interpretation was not.

Both causal models — “blunted response reduces switching” and “impaired splicing blunts the response” — predict this same correlation. With two conditions and n = 3 there is no design-based way to separate them. The numbers stay on the record; they are not evidence that the deficit is an artefact.

The HT arm of this control (crude OR 2.29, MH 2.49) is not shown here and should not be cited. H_HT is the one dataset that had a batch correction applied, so its switching rate is not on the same scale as T_HT’s; and its three-donor, three-day design means its rate answers a different question from T_HT’s one-genotype, one-day rate. That contrast is retired rather than recomputed — see docs/REVIEW_CHANGES.md §0g.

6.2 Switching genes strongly co-occur between genotypes

Genes that switch in one genotype are far more likely to switch in the other than chance allows — 15 observed against 0.6 expected. The knockout is not switching a different set of genes; it is switching fewer of the same ones.

6.3 When the same isoform is measurable in both, direction is preserved

This is the cleanest comparison available, because it selects on the outcome only once. Of isoforms significant in wildtype and measurable in the knockout, 85.0% move in the same direction — but only 22.9% reach the effect-size threshold there. The reciprocal is 78.9% and 32.9%.

That asymmetry is the crux: direction is preserved, magnitude is blunted.

6.4 What the isoform-level classification shows

The great majority of genotype-specific switches are not cases where the transcript is missing from the other genotype. It is there, it is measured, and its ratio holds. Only 6 isoforms are genuinely undetected in the opposite genotype.

6.4.1 What kind of transcript switches, and does it differ by group?

If genotype-specific switches were driven by a different kind of transcript than shared ones — say, more novel splicing — that would be a mechanistic clue. gffcompare class codes let us ask directly: = means the intron chain matches a reference transcript exactly, j means a novel splice-junction combination, and c means the model is contained within a reference transcript (a shorter, often fragmentary model).

Three things come out of this, and the second is the one worth remembering:

  1. Composition does differ overall (omnibus p = 0.045), and the Shared-versus-KO-only contrast is p = 0.010. Neither survives Bonferroni correction across the five tests, and under BH both sit at 0.099. Treat as suggestive.

  2. It is not about novel splicing. The novel-junction (j) fraction is statistically indistinguishable across groups — 22.2% shared, 11.2% WT-only, 6.6% KO-only, with Fisher p = 0.25 and 0.07 for the focused 2×2 tests. Whatever separates a reproducible switch from a genotype-specific one, it is not how novel the splicing is.

  3. What actually differs is transcript-model completeness. Contained (c) models — shorter fragments nested inside a reference transcript — make up 20.0% of WT-only and 27.9% of KO-only switches, but 0 of 18 shared switches. With n = 18 the 95% CI on that zero is 0–18.5%, so the difference is real but not tightly bounded.

The cautious reading: a fraction of single-genotype switches involve structurally lower-confidence transcript models, and those are exactly the calls that do not reproduce in the other genotype. That is as much a quality-control observation as a biological one — it suggests treating c-class genotype-specific switches as the lowest-priority tier for follow-up, and it makes the shared set (all = or j, no fragments) look like the more trustworthy core.

6.5 Seeing it gene by gene

Both arms are headed by inflammatory genes — CCL22, IL23A, CCL4, CD86, KDM6B, RSAD2 — again consistent with switching tracking the LPS program rather than drifting.

7 Pathway enrichment: a mostly negative result

With a real tested background available for all four datasets, enrichment can finally be run honestly. The universe is the genes quantified and tested in that same experiment — never the whole genome (which would treat unexpressed genes as failed candidates) and never the pre-reduced object (which would compare a significant set against a significant set).

Four of the seven gene sets return nothing at all — including the two largest genotype-specific sets (120 T-only and 53 U-only genes). That is a real finding: switches that occur in only one genotype are not a coherent functional group.

Where terms do appear, they are all the same thing:

WarningA big term count is not a big finding

The shared UT set returns 82 enriched terms from 15 genes, which looks impressive until you ask which genes produce them. Only 10 genes appear in any enriched term, and five — CCL3, CCL4, CCL22, IL23A, UTS2 — account for 95% of all gene-term hits. GO and Reactome are nested hierarchies, so one tight functional module generates dozens of overlapping terms. This is a chemokine/cytokine signal counted many times, not a broad functional program.

results/tables/pathway_enrichment_driver_summary.csv reports this alongside every term count for exactly this reason.

So the honest summary is: isoform switching after LPS is not enriched for coherent pathways beyond a small chemokine/cytokine core, and that core is shared between genotypes rather than specific to either. This is worth stating plainly, because the opposite result is what you would get from a careless background — testing these gene lists against all human genes would return the entire inflammatory-response hierarchy, and it would be an artefact of comparing expressed genes to unexpressed ones.

It also fits the picture from §6: the switches that reproduce across conditions are the core inflammatory ones; everything else is heterogeneous.

8 Interferon-response genes are where this concentrates

Section 7 asked an open question and got a mostly negative answer. This asks a closed one: take a curated interferon gene set and test it once per dataset against the same tested background. GO’s hierarchy scatters interferon biology across dozens of overlapping terms, so an open enrichment scan both dilutes and double-counts it.

Isoform switching is ~6–7× over-represented among interferon-response genes in the wildtype THP-1 datasets and in the knockout. This is the one clear positive signal in the project, and it is exactly where a cursory look suggested it would be.

WarningT_HT and T_UT agreeing is technical reproducibility, not biological replication

They are the same libraries (see §6.1), so their two odds ratios are one biological result observed twice — their switching ISGs overlap 7 of 9 in the union. The independent observations are U_UT (OR 6.2) and H_HT. The q column corrects across all rows as if independent and is therefore optimistic; q_within_library_group is also written to isg_enrichment.csv.

Counts are small throughout — 8, 8, 4 and 3 switching ISGs — which is why they are shown beside every odds ratio.

Splitting by interferon type, the type II (IFN-γ) set carries it:

Type II is significant in all three enriched datasets (OR 8.1, 8.0, 9.8). Type I is significant only in T_HT.

8.1 Which genes, and how consistent

Two things stand out. The gene identities are highly consistent across datasets — CCL3, CCL4, CCL22, IFITM2, GBP1, USP18, RAB7B, SHFL, IFIT1 recur. And almost every switching ISG involves a novel PacBio isoform; SHFL is the sole exception. Whatever is happening to interferon-response genes here is happening on transcript models that a short-read annotation would not contain.

8.2 T versus H, and WT versus knockout

In the UT pair the three ISGs switching in the knockout — CCL22, CCL3, CCL4, all chemokines — are all shared with wildtype, and each is larger in the knockout (CCL22 0.36→0.88, CCL4 0.19→0.32). The five wildtype-only ISGs (GBP1, IFITM2, RAB7B, SHFL, USP18) are the non-chemokine arm. Consistent with that, ISG switches in the knockout are markedly larger than non-ISG switches there (median |dIF| 0.39 vs 0.19, Wilcoxon p = 0.004) — the only dataset where that holds.

WarningTwo tempting patterns that do not survive testing

Both of these look compelling in the tables and should not be claimed:

  • “The knockout loses type I but keeps type II.” Zero type I ISGs switch in U_UT, but at that dataset’s background rate only 0.28 were expected anyway. Against T_UT (3 of 63) the difference gives Fisher p = 0.24 — not distinguishable.
  • “H doesn’t show the ISG signal.” H_HT gives OR 1.17 (q = 0.75), but the difference from T_HT’s OR 7.0 is p = 0.23. Part of the null is that H has a higher overall switching rate (2.08% vs 0.83%), so the same ISG count is less exceptional against its own background.

Counts per cell are single digits. The enrichment itself is solid; the between-dataset contrasts are not powered.

8.3 What would sharpen this

The gene sets here are GO “response to interferon” terms, which include upstream signalling components (CDC37, FADD, HDAC4) as well as induced effectors. A functional list — Schoggins or Interferome — is a tighter definition of an ISG and would likely raise the odds ratios. isg.custom_set_path in config takes a CSV of symbols, and nothing else in 07 changes.

9 Where the analysis is currently blind

9.1 What replication can possibly look like: the same-sample comparison

T_HT and T_UT are the same six sequencing libraries quantified against two different reference transcriptomes — identical replicate sample names including S-numbers, and gene-level expression correlating at r ≈ 0.99 for matched samples. Biological variability between them is zero, so every disagreement is annotation plus thresholding. Nothing in the project had noted this; it is the best technical control available.

One limit on how far this generalises. The two references are not the same transcript space viewed twice: HT merges the T and H PacBio transcripts, UT merges T and U. So part of the disagreement below is a genuine difference in annotation space, not measurement noise — which is why the number that follows is a useful reference point but not a “reproducibility ceiling”, as an earlier version of this document called it.

Agreement is far above chance (55 shared against 1.04 expected) and gene-level effect sizes track closely (Spearman 0.77). But the Jaccard is only 0.35.

Median |dIF| in the non-calling reference is 0.132 against a 0.15 cutoff, and 72% of discordant genes reach at least 0.10. So this is threshold brittleness rather than contradiction — but it means a single-dataset switching call carries roughly a one-in-three chance of not replicating under re-annotation alone.

ImportantJudge every replication rate against this number, not against 100%

This reframes numbers reported elsewhere in this document. The 6.1% T→H replication below is low against 100%; against the same-sample figure of 35% it is still low, but the gap is far smaller than it first appears. Read it as a reference point, not a ceiling: some of that 65% disagreement is annotation-space difference between the two references rather than irreducible noise.

9.2 Q1’s cross-genotype comparison, now with a proper denominator

Unfiltered exports for both HT datasets are now in place, which changes this section from “unusable” to “usable in both directions, and the answer is not what the biased version suggested”.

Switching genes co-occur between the two HT genotypes above chance (OR 5.4), but far less strongly than the two UT arms did (OR 36.1). That ordering makes sense: T_UT and U_UT differ only by the UBL5 knockout, whereas T_HT and H_HT are different genotypes.

ImportantA replication rate that was inflated ~8-fold

Judging only by what survived H_HT’s reduction, 6 of 105 T-significant isoforms were also significant in H — an apparent replication of 6%. But an isoform only stayed in that object if its gene was already significant there.

Against the 105 isoforms actually tested in H, the rate is 5.7%.

So LPS-driven switches in THP-1 are largely not reproduced as significant events in the H genotype — and the reciprocal is weaker still:

  • Direction is preserved well above chance in both directions — 81.9% T→H (86 of 105, binomial p = 2.3e-11) and 64.2% H→T (115 of 179, p = 0.00017).
  • But magnitude collapses: median |dIF| of 0.07 and 0.04 in the opposite dataset, with only 16.2% and 6.7% clearing the 0.15 threshold.

This is the same signature seen in the UBL5 arm, and more extreme: direction preserved, magnitude far below the calling threshold. Whether that reflects genuine genotype-specific attenuation or differences in power between the two runs cannot be settled here — H_HT actually has more significant isoforms overall (192 vs 125), which argues against simple underpowering.

20 T-significant isoforms are not detected in H at all and remain genuinely uninformative.

9.3 Statistics that did not survive scrutiny

Two results reported earlier in the project’s history do not hold up and have been removed or corrected:

  • A Fisher test of switching co-occurrence with OR 15.0, p = 0.031. Its background was 25 genes, all already significant by construction. Removed; the OR 36.1 result in §6.2 is its legitimate replacement on a 11,126-gene denominator.
  • An apparent finding that shared switches have larger effect sizes (Kruskal p = 9.3e-5) was an artefact: the shared group was summarised with pmax(WT, KO) while the genotype-specific groups used a single value. With each isoform measured in one genotype, the effect is no longer significant (p = 0.013).

Both are recorded in docs/REVIEW_CHANGES.md with evidence.

10 Where this leaves us

Q1 — Yes, and on the right genes. LPS drives isoform switching in 95 genes in wildtype THP-1, and the strongest events sit on canonical LPS-response genes. Novel long-read isoforms participate at full effect size, which justifies the PacBio-augmented reference. Against the H genotype, only 5.7% of those switches reproduce as significant, but 82% share direction at sub-threshold magnitude — the same attenuation signature as the UBL5 arm.

Q2 — UBL5 loss dampens rather than redirects. Three independent lines point the same way:

  1. Fewer genes switch in the knockout (16.4% vs 24.9% of tested genes).
  2. Switching genes strongly co-occur between genotypes (OR 36.1), so the knockout is not switching a different programme.
  3. Isoform-level direction is preserved (85.0% concordant) while magnitude falls below threshold in a third of cases.

The consistent reading is a quantitative attenuation of LPS-driven isoform selection, not a qualitative rewiring. That is compatible with UBL5 acting as a modulator of splicing efficiency rather than as a switch between alternative programmes — though the design here cannot demonstrate mechanism.

10.1 Honest limits

  • Every significance call comes from upstream ISA runs; this analysis inherits their model assumptions and power.
  • The WT-versus-KO significance-rate comparison spans two separate tests and is power-sensitive.
  • Concordance statistics rest on small matched sets (n = 140 and 76), because only isoforms measurable in both contribute.
  • Three replicates per condition. Sample names (T1_minus/T1_plus) suggest a paired design, but nothing in the pipeline passes a blocking factor and 02d’s noise model pools within-condition SD without using pairing. If the design is genuinely paired, a paired analysis would gain real power at n = 3 — which matters given the abundance floor removes a third to a half of calls. This needs confirming with whoever ran the experiment; it is not safe to infer from filenames, so nothing has been changed.
  • Switching is tail behaviour, not typical. Among isoforms above the abundance floor with mid-range fractions, the 99th percentile of |dIF| is 0.147 (T_HT), 0.153 (T_UT), 0.134 (U_UT) and 0.201 (H_HT). The 0.15 cutoff sits at roughly the 99th percentile of the whole distribution, so calls come from the extreme tail where estimator error dominates — consistent with the ~35% same-sample agreement above.
  • Pathway enrichment is now implemented (§7) and is largely negative. The one positive signal rests on five genes, so it should not be over-read.

10.2 Next steps, in priority order

  1. Targeted validation of the dampening model — a handful of high-|dIF| WT switches that fail threshold in the knockout (CD86 is a natural first candidate) by isoform-specific qPCR.
  2. Novel-isoform follow-up on the j-class switching transcripts, which are the ones a short-read annotation would have missed entirely.
  3. Isoform-level functional consequence. Pathway enrichment on gene lists cannot see what a switch does — two isoforms of the same gene sit in the same GO terms. ISA’s domain/NMD/coding-potential annotations are the natural next question, and would say whether these switches change protein output rather than merely which transcript carries it.
